abstract: This Harvard Business School working paper examines whether generative AI displaces workers or augments their jobs by analyzing labor demand and skill requirements across occupations. Using O*NET v25.1 and US job postings data from LightCast (2019 to June 2024), the authors identify a dual, heterogeneous impact: automation-prone occupations see reduced demand while augmentation-prone occupations see increased demand.
keyFindings: 24% decrease in generative AI-exposed skills per firm per quarter for occupations in the top quartile of automation potential after ChatGPT launch
15% increase in generative AI-exposed skills per firm per quarter for augmentation-prone occupations
Similar trends mirrored in both total number of required skills and newly required skills across job postings
Generative AI simplifies tasks in automation-prone occupations while enhancing productivity and skill requirements in augmentation-prone roles
methodology: Analysis of O*NET v25.1 database and US job postings data from LightCast covering the period from 2019 to June 2024. Occupations classified into automation-prone and augmentation-prone categories based on task exposure to generative AI capabilities.
qualifiers: Data covers only the period through June 2024, relatively early in the generative AI adoption cycle. Job posting data may not fully reflect actual hiring outcomes. The dual effect (displacement + complementarity) means net employment impact depends on the relative size of each channel.
